title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, Benchmarks, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s canonical serving runtime reference: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes for the runtime, known issues and mitigation, operational runbooks, and team wiki links. It is intended for engineers who operate or extend the serving runtime, SREs troubleshooting production regressions, and program managers planning performance work.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: all components of the serving runtime (request router, model execution pool, KV cache, batching subsystem, kernel selection layer, and telemetry hooks).
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra SREs, applied ML (model-onboarding), and performance-focused product engineers.

1) Runtime architecture (overview)

Goal: provide a high-level map of runtime components, data flows, ownership, and SLOs.

High-level components:
- Request ingress (API gateway / frontend): handles auth, rate limits, tenant routing.
- Router & policy layer: evaluates routing policy (latency tier, cost tier, region, model variant) and selects the target serving pool.
- Serving pool (executor nodes): GPU-backed workers running the inference engine. Each node manages multiple model shards and handles KV cache and batching.
- Batching manager: coalesces compatible requests (model id, precision, max tokens) into micro-batches.
- Kernel selection & execution planner: picks optimized kernels/graph plan per layer based on architecture, sequence length distribution, and quantization profile.
- KV cache & prefix cache: shared within a model-session to speed up decoding; TTL and eviction policies are described below.
- Observability & tracing: per-request trace, token-level latency, GPU utilization, and per-model quality metrics (where available).

Data flows and interactions:
1. Ingress validates request and forwards to router.
2. Router applies policy; assigns request to a serving pool and optional fallback model variant.
3. Serving node queues request in its batching manager. If batching window/threshold hits, a micro-batch is constructed.
4. Execution planner selects kernels; decoder runs using KV cache when applicable.
5. Response streams back via router and frontend. Metrics emitted at each hop.

SLOs (runtime-wide):
- P95 response latency (single-turn, <=128 prompt tokens): <= 120 ms for tier-1 models on dedicated nodes.
- P99 tail latency: <= 350 ms.
- Token generation throughput (per-GPU): target depends on instance type; see benchmarking table in section 4.
- Availability (regional): 99.95% for Dedicated pools (SLA-backed).

Ownership and contacts:
- Runtime architecture owner: eng-serving-runtime (team owner: runtime-core). Primary contact: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.example).
- Kernel scheduling and perf lead: Diego Morales.
- SRE escalation: ops-sre@redwood.example.

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies

Design goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs.
- Minimize model variance: deterministic kernel choice for a given model configuration and sequence-length distribution unless explicitly overridden.
- Fall back gracefully to compatible kernels when new kernels are experimental.

Scheduling primitives:
- Execution lanes: logical queues per model-precision pair (e.g., gpt-4-xl/4bit).
- Priority classes: realtime (interactive, low-latency), batch (background long-running), preemptible (spot/burst).
- Batching policies: per-lane min-batch and max-batch, max-latency-window (ms).

Kernel selection algorithm (high level):
1. Lookup model profile (metadata: architecture, supported kernels, quantization profile, preferred workspace sizes).
2. Check input sequence length; normalize to sampling bucket (e.g., 1–64, 65–128, 129–512).
3. Query device capability table for the node (SM count, memory, supported instruction sets).
4. Score candidate kernels by expected per-token latency and memory headroom. Score = alpha * latency_est + beta * memory_penalty + gamma * failure_risk.
5. Select kernel with minimum score that satisfies safety headroom. If score delta to next-best < threshold, prefer stable kernel.

Safety and circuit breakers:
- Kernel health table: tracks recent kernel failures, OOMs, and numeric anomalies. Kernels with >5% failure rate in 1h window are auto-flagged and avoided.
- OOM guard: if a planned run would exceed 85% GPU memory usage, scheduler rejects kernel choice and tries a lower-memory kernel or signals fallback to a smaller model variant.

Tuning knobs (config table):
- min_batch_size: integer (default 1 for realtime lanes).
- max_batch_size: integer (default 32).
- max_batch_wait_ms: integer (default 12 ms).
- kernel_score_weights: string (alpha,beta,gamma).
- oom_memory_threshold_pct: integer (default 85).

3) Profiling playbook (how-to run perf investigations)

When to run profiling:
- Regressions in P95/P99 latency observed for a model or pool.
- New kernel or driver release deployed.
- Model onboarding with unknown performance characteristics.

Quick checklist (triage):
1. Confirm the scope: model id, instance type, region, observed window, and SLO signal (latency or throughput).
2. Reproduce in canary/bench cluster if possible with same request mix.
3. Capture traces: enable per-request tracing and collect flamegraphs (see commands below).
4. Capture GPU state: nvidia-smi, nvprof / Nsight snapshots, and device power/temperature.
5. Check kernel health table and runtime logs for OOMs or kernel falling back.

Common tools and commands:
- Request replay (bench tool): 
  ./bench/replay --model MODEL_ID --trace trace-YYYYMMDD.json --rate 50 --duration 300
- Collect per-request trace (on node): 
  curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/debug/trace?request_id=<id>" -o /tmp/trace-<id>.json
- Produce flamegraph (on trace): 
  python tools/trace_to_flame.py /tmp/trace-<id>.json > /tmp/flame-<id>.svg
- GPU snapshot: 
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 5 -o TD > /tmp/gpu-dmon.log &
  ncu --target-processes all --section sm -o /tmp/ncu-snapshot

Profiling checklist (in-depth):
- Step 1: Validate workload characteristics (prompt distribution, token distribution, streaming vs non-streaming).
- Step 2: Confirm batching behavior (are requests being batched as expected? any fragmentation?).
- Step 3: Examine kernel selection decisions and evaluate alternative kernels in bench environment.
- Step 4: Run microbenchmarks (single request end-to-end, kernel-only tests, KV cache hit vs miss).
- Step 5: If OOMs: collect heap/gpu memory timelines, reduce batch size or quantize more aggressively, or route to higher-memory node.

Measurement artifacts to collect:
- request_trace.json, kernel_choice.log, gpu-dmon.log, ncu report, bench replay config, and system journal logs. Attach to incident or perf ticket.

4) Benchmarking suite and results (how we measure performance)

Benchmark goals:
- Provide reproducible per-model per-instance throughput and latency baselines across sequence-length buckets and precision (fp16, int8, 4bit).
- Provide unit economics (tokens/sec and $/k-token) for standard instance types.

Bench harness components:
- Traffic generator: bench/replay (see commands above). Supports request distributions, streaming toggles, and payload variance.
- Microbench: kernel-only harness to measure convolution/attention kernels in isolation.
- Orchestrator: reproduces a multi-tenant mix against a dedicated pool with configurable admission control.

Representative results (excerpt):
- Instance type: RTX-A5000 (40 GB)
  - gpt-4-small (fp16), seq_len=128: 850 tokens/sec (per-GPU), P95 token latency 8 ms
  - gpt-4-small (4bit), seq_len=128: 1200 tokens/sec, P95 token latency 6 ms
- Instance type: H100-80GB
  - gpt-4-xl (fp16), seq_len=128: 4200 tokens/sec, P95 token latency 4.5 ms
  - gpt-4-xl (4bit), seq_len=128: 5200 tokens/sec, P95 token latency 3.8 ms

How to run full benchmark suite:
1. Provision a bench cluster via infra job: infra/provision_bench.sh --pool bench-rt-1 --instance h100-family --nodes 4
2. Deploy latest runtime image: deploy/runtime:bench-<sha>
3. Execute suite: ./bench/run_suite --suite full --output results/YYYYMMDD --concurrency 256
4. Upload results to perf dashboard: ./tools/upload_perf.py results/YYYYMMDD --dashboard perf/runtime

Benchmark reporting and CI:
- Nightly microbench runs (per-commit) are executed in CI; results are compared to baseline and flagged if any regression > 3% for P95 token latency.
- Weekly full-suite runs for each target instance family; regressions create a perf-alert ticket automatically.

5) Release notes (recent notable changes)

2029-02-28 (v3.14.0):
- Kernel: introduced fused-attention v2 kernel for causal decoding with improved memory locality; reduces P95 token latency by ~7% for long sequences.
- Scheduler: new adaptive-batching mode (experimental) that adjusts max_batch_wait_ms based on recent latency pressure. Disabled by default.
- Observability: added token-level rate breakdown to per-route dashboard.
- Known issues: on some A5000 drivers 535.x, fused-attention v2 can trigger a rare SM hang; auto-rollback gate prevents rollout to affected fleets.

2028-10-12 (v3.10.1):
- Fixed a regression where KV cache TTL was not honored across model warm restarts.
- Improved kernel_score_weights default to favor stable kernels under high contention.

6) Known issues and mitigations (current as of last_updated)

KI-3211: Fused-attention v2 hang on A5000 drivers 535.x
- Symptoms: node stops making progress on decoding, request-level timeouts, GPU SM utilization stuck.
- Mitigation: scheduler automatically flags fused-attention v2 on nodes with driver 535.x and routes to fallback kernel. Operators: roll back driver to 532.x or disable fused-attention v2 rollout.

KI-4287: Increased batching fragmentation for multi-tenant pools with high variance token length
- Symptoms: lower-than-expected batching efficiency, throughput drop.
- Mitigation: tune per-lane max_batch_wait_ms up to 25 ms for mixed workloads; consider workload isolation into separate pools.

KI-5020: Memory regression after runtime container image 3.12.0
- Symptoms: slight increase in peak resident GPU memory due to buffer alignment changes.
- Mitigation: use runtime image 3.11.x for affected customers; patch queued in release 3.14.1.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

A. Incident — high tail latency for a model
1. Confirm alert and scope (which model, pool, region).
2. Check recent deploys: github release pinned to runtime image or kernel rollout.
3. Run bench/replay against canary using observed traffic mix.
4. Inspect kernel health table and node OOM logs.
5. If kernel failure: toggle rollout to previous kernel in rollout service.
6. If noisy neighbor suspected: identify top tenants by token/sec and apply temporary admission control on offending tenant.
7. Communicate to customer success for impacted tenants (if dedicated).

B. Incident — GPU OOMs reported
1. Identify process and model causing OOM in dmesg/journal.
2. Lower max_batch_size on lane to safe default (e.g., from 32 to 8).
3. If persistent, point traffic to larger-instance pool or enable 4bit quantized variant.
4. Create perf ticket to investigate memory regression.

C. Routine — run a perf regression check after a kernel or driver update
1. Schedule bench run for representative models (short, medium, long).
2. Compare P95/P99 to baseline and verify token-per-second targets.
3. Approve rollout if within thresholds; otherwise halt rollout and triage.

Playbook escalation contacts:
- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.example (pager duty).
- Kernel lead: Diego Morales (diego@redwood.example).

Onboarding notes for new hires:
- Read the architecture and runbooks top-to-bottom.
- Run the bench replay with the sample trace and reproduce a non-streaming decode.
- Pair with a runtime engineer to walk a real incident postmortem.

Appendix A — Config reference (examples)

Example lane config (YAML-like):
lane_id: realtime-gpt4-small
model_id: gpt-4-small
min_batch_size: 1
max_batch_size: 16
max_batch_wait_ms: 12
priority: realtime
quantization_profile: 4bit-recommended

Example kernel_score_weights: "alpha=0.7,beta=0.2,gamma=0.1"

Appendix B — Diagnostic checklist to attach to perf tickets
- bench replay config
- request_trace.json and flamegraph.svg
- kernel_choice.log and kernel_health snapshot
- gpu-dmon.log and ncu report
- node journal and container logs

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-core).
- Review cadence: quarterly or on any major runtime/kernel release.
- To propose changes: open a docs PR against confluence source and request reviewers (Diego Morales, Rina Gupta).

If you find missing examples or need a small reproducer, reach out to the runtime team in #runtime-help on Slack or file an internal ticket (TKT-RT-XXXX).
